draft.title: Reading financial trends
card: Line graphs
Financial data such as share prices and exchange rates is often shown on a line graph. Time is on the horizontal axis and the value is on the vertical axis.
Trend
A line that rises over time shows an increase. A line that falls shows a decrease. The size of the change is the later value minus the earlier value.
Percentage change
Percentage change = change ÷ starting value × 100. Example: a share price goes from $20 to $25. The change is 5, and 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%.
Exchange rate
An exchange rate says how much of one currency buys another. If A$1 = US$0.60, then A$100 buys 100 × 0.60 = US$60.
draft.remember: Read the change from the graph, then divide by the starting value for a percentage.

a.q: A share price rises from $40 to $50. What is the percentage increase?
a.why: The change is 50 − 40 = 10. Then 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%. 20% is wrong because it divides by the new price instead of the starting price.
a.clue: Divide the change by the starting value.

b.q: The exchange rate is A$1 = 0.65 euros. Sam changes A$200 into euros. How many euros does he get?
b.why: Each Australian dollar buys 0.65 euros, so 200 × 0.65 = 130 euros. Dividing 200 by 0.65 gives 307.69, which uses the rate the wrong way round.
b.clue: Multiply the dollars by the euros bought per dollar.

problems.detail: The exchange rate definition, 'how much of one currency buys another', is vague. It could be read as the reverse of the example's direction. Clearer: 'how much of one currency you get for one unit of another'.

check.summary: Both questions and their explanations are correct: 25% and 130 euros. The only issue is a slightly vague exchange-rate definition on the card, which the example clarifies.

card: Line graphs

Percentage change \(=\) change \(\div\) starting value \(\times 100\). Example: a share price goes from $20 to $25. The change is $5, and \(\$5 \div \$20 \times 100 = 25\%\).
